name: Harshnag
equipment: A tattered frost giant-sized cloak worn as a blanket
Whetstone carved from glacial ice (never melts)
A set of bone dice carved from mammoth ivory
Rank insignia from the Gray Hands of Waterdeep
A small iron figurine of Thrym, god of frost giants (kept but not worshipped)
features: Fighting Style: Great Weapon Fighting (reroll 1s and 2s on damage dice with two-handed melee weapons)
Second Wind (bonus action, regain 1d10+5 HP, 1/short rest)
Action Surge (take one additional action on your turn, 1/short rest)
Extra Attack (attack twice when taking the Attack action)
Improved Critical (weapon attacks score a critical hit on a roll of 19 or 20)

Runt's Resilience (advantage on saving throws against being frightened by creatures larger than you — born the smallest of his frost giant clan, Harshnag learned early to stand firm when towering figures tried to intimidate him)

Giant's Insight (1/long rest, as a reaction when an ally makes an Intelligence (History) or Wisdom (Insight) check related to giant culture, the Ordning, or giant-kin behavior, grant that ally advantage on the check. Harshnag draws on decades of living in both worlds to provide crucial context.)
Frost Giant Endurance (resistance to cold damage — Harshnag's frost giant blood grants him the endurance of his kind, though diminished by his smaller stature)
Soldier: Military Rank (can invoke former rank among soldiers and veterans of Waterdeep's Gray Hands to secure minor assistance, lodging, or information)

Great Weapon Master (feat — before making a melee attack with a heavy weapon, can choose to take -5 to attack roll for +10 damage; on a critical hit or reducing a creature to 0 HP, can make one melee weapon attack as a bonus action)

Indomitable Spirit (Harshnag has weathered decades of rejection from both giant and small folk societies. Once per long rest, when he fails a Wisdom saving throw, he can reroll it and must use the new result.)

personality.traits: I speak rarely, but when I do, my words carry the weight of hard-won experience. I judge others by their actions, never their size or station. I find comfort in simple routines — sharpening my axe, watching the stars, sharing a quiet drink.
personality.ideals: Honor. A warrior's worth is measured not by the battles they win, but by the battles they choose to fight. I rejected the raiding and cruelty of my kin because honor demanded it, and I would make that choice again every time.
personality.bonds: I owe a life-debt to the people of Waterdeep who accepted me when my own kind cast me out. Princess Serissa of the storm giants called for aid, and I answered — because if the Ordning shatters completely, both giants and small folk will drown in the chaos. I will not let that happen.
personality.flaws: I carry a deep, quiet shame about my size — among frost giants, I am a runt, a disgrace. No matter how many battles I win among small folk, part of me still feels like the too-small child being mocked by his brothers. This makes me slow to trust praise and quick to shoulder burdens alone.

appearance: Harshnag stands just over seven feet tall — enormous by human standards, but pathetically small for a frost giant, where adults typically reach fifteen to twenty-one feet. His skin is a pale blue-gray, like winter sky before a storm, and his eyes are a deep, glacial blue that seem to hold centuries of cold patience. His hair is white as fresh snow, worn long and tied back in a single thick braid that reaches between his shoulder blades, interwoven with small iron rings — a frost giant tradition marking battles survived. His face is broad and craggy, etched with deep lines and old scars, particularly a long slash running from his left temple to his jaw — a parting gift from his eldest brother when Harshnag left the clan. His hands are massive, scarred, and calloused, each finger as thick as a human's wrist. He moves with a deliberate, measured grace that seems wrong for someone his size — decades among smaller folk taught him to be careful where he steps, what he touches, how much force he uses. He wears battered but well-maintained splint armor over layers of leather and fur, and a frost giant-sized cloak has been cut down and re-stitched (badly) to fit his frame, still dragging slightly on the ground behind him. His greataxe is sized for him — a human weapon, not a giant's — and he keeps it obsessively sharp. Around his neck hangs the iron insignia of the Gray Hands of Waterdeep, dull and worn but never removed.
backstory: Harshnag was born the smallest child of Jarl Krothgar's brood in the Spine of the World, a frost giant clan that measured worth in size and savagery. Where his brothers and sisters grew to fifteen, eighteen, twenty feet, Harshnag stopped at a pitiful seven. He was mocked relentlessly — called 'Runt,' 'Halfling,' and worse. His mother tried to protect him, but frost giant culture has no patience for weakness, and eventually even she turned away. Harshnag survived by being smarter, faster, and more ruthless than his siblings expected. He learned to fight not with the overwhelming force of a true frost giant but with technique, precision, and an understanding of leverage that his larger kin never needed to develop. But the raids broke him. When his clan descended on a Dwarvish mining settlement, Harshnag watched his brothers slaughter families — not for resources or territory, but for sport. He saw a dwarf mother shielding her children with her body, and something inside him shattered. He turned on his own clan mid-raid, buying the surviving dwarves time to flee. His eldest brother gave him the scar across his face and left him for dead in the snow. He was not dead. The dwarves he saved found him, and despite every reason to let a frost giant bleed out, they carried him to safety. That act of mercy — given to someone whose kind had just tried to murder them — changed Harshnag forever. He wandered south, eventually reaching Waterdeep, where the Lords' Alliance was cautiously willing to employ a frost giant who wanted to protect rather than destroy. He joined the Gray Hands, Waterdeep's elite adventuring force, and served with distinction for nearly two decades. He fought alongside humans, elves, dwarves, and halflings, and earned their trust through actions rather than words. When his service ended, he wandered again — a giant among small folk, too small for giants, belonging fully to neither world. Then the Ordning shattered. The ancient hierarchy that governed all giantkind collapsed, and every giant type began scrambling for supremacy. Storm giants withdrew. Fire giants began forging weapons of war. Hill giants descended on farming settlements in endless hunger. And Princess Serissa of the storm giants — the last voice of reason among her kind — sent out a desperate call for allies. Harshnag answered. Not because he loves giantkind — they cast him out — but because he understands both worlds, and he knows that if the giant crisis is not resolved, the destruction will consume everything he has come to care about. He is old now, by adventuring standards. His joints ache in cold weather (which is ironic for a frost giant). But his axe is sharp, his honor is intact, and he has one more fight left in him.

dmNotes.roleplaying: Harshnag is the party's anchor — steady, dependable, and deeply sad beneath his stoic exterior. Play him as a man of very few words who chooses each one carefully. He does not joke often, but when he does, it is bone-dry and delivered with a completely straight face. He defers to the party's decisions in most matters, but will speak up firmly and immovably when he believes innocent lives are at stake. In combat, he positions himself between danger and weaker party members without being asked — it is simply instinct. He never boasts about kills or victories. After a fight, he cleans his axe in silence. He is uncomfortable in crowded cities and taverns — too many staring faces, too many whispered comments about his size. He relaxes most in the wilderness, where size does not matter and the stars look the same as they did from the Spine of the World. He has a soft spot for children and small creatures, and will go out of his way to avoid frightening them. When the party encounters giants, Harshnag becomes visibly tense — these encounters force him to confront his identity crisis. He will try to negotiate first, always, but fights without hesitation if negotiation fails.
dmNotes.voice: Harshnag speaks in short, declarative sentences with a faint Norse-inflected cadence — he drops articles and uses formal constructions. His voice is a deep rumble, like distant thunder. He pauses often, choosing words with visible effort. Examples: 'Is not wise. Giants do not parley when blood is up. We go around.' / 'I have seen this before. Fire giants forge for war, not craft. What they build in Ironslag is meant to break walls.' / 'You ask why I left my kin. Is simple. They were wrong. Being large does not make you right. Being strong does not make you good. I learned this from a dwarf woman who was three feet tall and braver than any giant I have known.' / When angry (rare): 'No. This I will not allow. You will not touch them. Step back or I will move you.' / When sad (very rare, usually late at night): 'Sometimes I dream I am tall. Tall as my brothers. And they welcome me home. Then I wake, and I am still... this. It is enough. Most days, it is enough.' / When offering rare praise: 'You fought well today. Is good.'
dmNotes.motivations: Primary: Guide the party to the Eye of the All-Father, an ancient oracle temple in the Spine of the World, where they can learn the truth about why the Ordning shattered and how to restore it. He knows the location but has never been inside — the temple's guardians refused him entry because he is 'not giant enough.' Secondary: Protect the small folk settlements along the Sword Coast from giant raids — every village burned is a personal failure to him, a reminder of the dwarf settlement he could not save in time. Tertiary: Find peace with his identity. He is neither fully giant nor fully human, and decades of living between worlds have left him profoundly lonely. He will never admit this aloud, but the party's acceptance means more to him than he can express.
dmNotes.secrets: 1) Harshnag knows the exact location of the Eye of the All-Father oracle temple in the Spine of the World and the pass through the mountains to reach it — but he also knows the temple's rune-guardians will test anyone who enters, and the tests are lethal for the unworthy. He has not shared the details of these tests because he does not want to frighten the party away from the only lead they have. 2) During his time with the Gray Hands, Harshnag encountered a blue dragon disguised as a storm giant advisor. He could not prove it then and was dismissed as paranoid. That dragon was Iymrith. He suspects — but cannot confirm — that Iymrith is now embedded in the storm giant court, manipulating events from within. He will share this suspicion if the party earns his deep trust. 3) Harshnag carries a sealed letter from Serissa intended for the oracle at the Eye of the All-Father. He has not read it and will not open it — his honor forbids it. The letter contains Serissa's confession that she believes her own mother's disappearance was orchestrated by someone inside the storm giant court. 4) His frost giant clan, the Krothgar, are among the raiders currently attacking the Sword Coast. If the party encounters them, Harshnag will face his eldest brother Vjalgrim — the one who scarred him — and the confrontation will be deeply personal.
dmNotes.attitude: Harshnag is reserved but respectful with all party members from the start. He does not warm up quickly — trust must be earned through actions, not words. He responds best to competence, courage, and kindness toward the vulnerable. He has quiet respect for fighters and martial characters who understand discipline. He is uncomfortable around flashy magic users but recognizes their value. He is most open with characters who have experienced exile or rejection — shared outsider status creates an unspoken bond. He is protective of physically smaller party members without being condescending. He treats Felgolos with wary respect — bards make him nervous because they remind him of politics, but he senses Felgolos knows more than he lets on. He and Urgala share a soldier's mutual understanding — few words, total reliability. He finds Zephyros deeply unsettling because the wizard's fractured mind reminds him of what the Ordning's shattering has done to all giants. He respects Duvessa's intelligence but distrusts politicians on principle.
